extracted.intended_audience: parties and counsel participating in PTAB inter partes reviews (petitioners, patent owners, and their attorneys/experts)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used by the PTAB to evaluate patentability (obviousness, claim construction, motions, evidence, sealing) in an inter partes review final written decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail in this inter partes review of the challenged claims, Petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence. 35 U.S.C. § 316(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All factual findings and ultimate conclusions as to unpatentability are measured against the preponderance standard; cite supporting declarations/exhibits accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 and KSR
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter, as a whole, would have been obvious at the time of the invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art. KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply KSR principles (need for a reason to combine elements, not simply showing elements existed separately) and consider the whole-claim context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations, including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness. Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the strength of each Graham factor in every case; secondary considerations (objective indicia) must be considered and weighed (Stratoflex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine elements in the way the claimed invention does. A person of ordinary skill must have had a reasonable expectation of success. (KSR; PAR Pharm., Inc. v. TWi Pharms., Inc., 773 F.3d 1186 (Fed. Cir. 2014)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show documentary/technical reasons in the prior art or POSA knowledge that would motivate combining references and make success reasonably expected, not merely possible after-the-fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in IPR — broadest reasonable construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the Board interprets a claim term in an unexpired patent according to its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which it appears. 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Cuozzo Speed Techs., LLC v. Lee, 136 S. Ct. 2131 (2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill in the art in context of the entire patent disclosure; special definitions must be clear, deliberate, and precise (Paulsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prosecution history in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is construed with reference to the prosecution history to exclude interpretations disclaimed during prosecution; statements during prosecution can be relevant to reinforce the meaning of claim language. (Graham; Chimie v. PPG; D’Agostino; Microsoft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant expressly defined a term during prosecution (e.g., specified a comparator), the Board will give effect to that choice; prosecution statements can bind claim scope or at least reinforce interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim terms need only be construed as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms need only be construed to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy. Wellman, Inc. v. Eastman Chem. Co., 642 F.3d 1355 (Fed. Cir. 2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-interpret terms; construe only those needed to decide patentability issues before the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness and applicant as lexicographer (35 U.S.C. § 112 issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may reject claims as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112; an applicant may overcome such a rejection by providing a specific definition for a claim term in prosecution (applicant may be his own lexicographer). Paulsen, 30 F.3d 1475.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution admissions and responses can define claim scope for later IPR construction; the Board will respect such special definitions even if they lead to odd results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on new matter in motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to amend is subject to the statutory and regulatory prohibition on introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. § 316(d)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a)(2)(ii) (no new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed substitute claims must have adequate written-description support in the original disclosure (specification/provisional); if substitute claim introduces new matter, motion to amend must be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on motions to amend — single motion and good-cause requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider a single motion to amend under 35 U.S.C. § 316(d)(1) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a); the Board may authorize a second motion only if Patent Owner establishes the 'good cause showing' required in 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If seeking to file an additional motion to amend after authorization, the movant must first show good cause per the regulation; failure to establish good cause precludes filing the second motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse judgment by party (requesting judgment against itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may request judgment against itself at any time during a proceeding. 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(b). Section 42.73(a) requires that a 'judgment' disposes of all issues that were, or reasonably could have been raised or decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner can request partial adverse judgment (e.g., withdraw a ground) and SAS/Office guidance confirms a petitioner can request adverse judgment on claims/grounds; Board will consider scope implications and final decision must dispose of issues as required by rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of SAS/Institution scope on final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner's contentions define the scope of the litigation from institution through conclusion; after SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu, only claims still challenged by the petitioner at the end must be addressed in the Board’s final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners can limit scope post-institution by withdrawing grounds or requesting adverse judgment; Board follows USPTO SAS Q&As in applying procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witness admissibility and qualification (Rule 702 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert witness must be qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education to testify in the form of an opinion. Fed. R. Evid. 702. There is no requirement of a perfect match between the expert’s experience and the relevant field; the expert must be 'qualified in the pertinent art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will consider qualifications and relevance; lack of exact POSA match goes to weight, not necessarily admissibility. Demonstrate relevant experience, publications, collaboration, and relevance to issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to exclude evidence — relevance and weight considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence may be excluded under Federal Rules (FRE 402, 403, 602, 801, 802) if irrelevant or otherwise inadmissible; inconsistencies in witness testimony generally go to weight, not admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moving to exclude, explain legal basis (e.g., hearsay, lack of personal knowledge). If witness gave deposition and supplemental declarations, Board may deny exclusion and leave inconsistencies for weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for sealing materials in IPRs — good cause and confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong public policy for making IPR materials public (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(1); 37 C.F.R. § 42.14). A party may move to seal certain information, but only 'confidential information' (trade secret or other confidential research, development, or commercial information) is protected. 37 C.F.R. § 42.2. The standard for granting a motion to seal is 'for good cause.' 37 C.F.R. § 42.54(a). The movant bears the burden to explain why the information is confidential. 37 C.F.R. § 42.20(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific, narrowly tailored justification showing material constitutes confidential business information and why public disclosure would harm competitive interests; generic claims are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest and timing for disclosure of sealed materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information subject to a protective order ordinarily becomes public 45 days after final judgment in a trial (Trial Practice Guide). There is an expectation that confidential information relied upon or identified in a final written decision will be made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party wants to maintain confidentiality of material discussed in the final written decision, file a timely renewed motion to seal that provides justification outweighing the public interest and supply narrowly redacted public versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and admissibility of abstracts and preliminary disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts and conference abstracts (e.g., Baselga '94) may be considered prior art (printed publication) and can be relied upon; POSAs often apply information in abstracts before full peer-reviewed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on abstracts, provide corroborating evidence (publication/authorship, subsequent citations) and explain why a POSA would consider the abstract sufficiently credible and motivating to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining level of ordinary skill in the art (POSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a person of ordinary skill in the art for Graham factor analysis; if not disputed, Board may adopt the parties' agreed definition. Prior art itself can reflect appropriate skill level. (Okajima; Litton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the POSA (e.g., clinical oncologist with years of breast cancer research) and rely on prior art evidence to support the characterization rather than requiring extensive separate findings when the record is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining references — cannot win by attacking references individually
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-obviousness cannot be established by attacking references individually where the patentability challenge is based upon the teachings of a combination of references. In re Keller, 642 F.2d 413 (CCPA 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting obviousness based on multiple references, show how the references collectively teach or motivate the claimed combination; attacking each reference separately is insufficient.
